cues.text: ODYSSEY — BOOK IV
Sparta: Helen and Menelaus remember Troy;\nProteus; the suitors set their ambush.
And they came to hollow Lacedaemon, land of ravines,\nand drove to the house of glorious Menelaus.
They found him giving a wedding-feast to his many kinsmen
for his son and his blameless daughter, in his own house.
The daughter he was sending to the\nson of Achilles, breaker of ranks:
in Troy long ago he had promised her, had bowed his head
to give her, and now the gods were\nbringing the marriage to pass.
So now with horses and chariots he was sending her forth
to the famous city of the Myrmidons, whom that man ruled.
For his son he was bringing home\nAlector's daughter out of Sparta —
the son born to him in his strength,\nwell-loved Megapenthes,
out of a slave-woman. For to Helen\nthe gods showed no more children
after the first time, when she bore her lovely daughter\nHermione, who had the beauty of golden Aphrodite.
So they were feasting through the great high-roofed house,\nthe neighbors and kinsmen of glorious Menelaus,
taking their pleasure; and among them a godlike\nsinger sang to the lyre, and two tumblers among them,
as he led the song, went spinning through their midst.
And the two of them halted at the\ngateway of the house, themselves
and their horses — the hero\nTelemachus and Nestor's shining son.
Lord Eteoneus came out and saw them,\nthe busy henchman of glorious Menelaus,
and went through the house to bring\nthe news to the shepherd of the people;
standing close he spoke winged words to him:
"Two strangers here, Menelaus, nurtured of Zeus —\ntwo men, and they look like the stock of great Zeus.
Tell me: do we unyoke their swift horses for them,\nor send them on to another man, who may welcome them?"
Then fair-haired Menelaus, greatly stirred, replied:
"You were no fool before, Eteoneus, son of Boethous —\nbut now you are babbling nonsense like a child.
The two of us ate plenty of strangers' bread,\nyou and I, on the road home, hoping Zeus might someday
give us rest from misery. Unyoke the strangers' horses,
and bring the men themselves in, to share the feast."
So he spoke, and the man dashed back\nthrough the hall, and called the other
busy henchmen to come along with him.
They loosed the sweating horses from under the\nyoke and tied them up at the mangers of the horses,
and threw them spelt, and mixed white barley in with it,
and leaned the chariot against the gleaming entrance-wall,
and led the men into the godlike house. And they stared
in wonder through the house of the Zeus-nurtured king:
for there was a sheen as of the sun or the moon\nthrough the high-roofed house of glorious Menelaus.
And when they had had their joy of gazing,\nthey stepped into the polished baths and bathed.
And when the slave-women had bathed\nthem and rubbed them with oil,
and thrown about them fleecy cloaks and tunics,\nthey sat down on high seats beside Menelaus, Atreus' son.
A handmaid brought water for their hands in a pitcher,
a beautiful golden one, and poured it over a silver basin
for them to wash, and drew up\na polished table beside them.
The grave housekeeper brought\nbread and set it before them,
laying out delicacies in plenty, giving gladly of her\nstore; a carver lifted platters of meat of every kind
and set them down, and placed gold cups beside them.
And fair-haired Menelaus greeted\nthem with a wave of the hand:
"Take of the bread, and be welcome. And afterward,\nwhen you have tasted supper, we will ask what men
you are: for the stock of your parents is not lost in you —\nyou are of the stock of scepter-bearing kings,
nurtured of Zeus. No base men could father such sons."
So he spoke, and set before them\nthe fat roast chine of an ox,
lifting it in his hands —\nthe portion of honor they had set for him.
And their hands went out to the\ngood things spread before them.
But when they had put away desire for food and drink,\nthen Telemachus spoke to the son of Nestor,
leaning his head close, so that the others might not hear:
"Look, son of Nestor, delight of my heart —\nthe lightning of bronze through these echoing halls,
the gold and the amber, the silver and the ivory!
Such, I think, is the court of Olympian Zeus within:
all this here, past speaking!\nAwe takes me, looking at it."
But fair-haired Menelaus caught what he was saying,\nand lifting his voice he spoke winged words to them:
"Dear children, with Zeus no mortal man could vie:
his halls and his possessions are deathless things.
Among men, another may match me in wealth — or may not.
Much I suffered for it, and far I wandered to bring\nit home in my ships: eight years gone before I came,
driven wandering to Cyprus and\nPhoenicia and the Egyptians;
I reached the Ethiopians, the Sidonians, the Erembi,\nand Libya, where the lambs come horned from the birth,
for the ewes bear three times\nin the full round of the year.
There no lord and no shepherd goes wanting\nfor cheese and meat and sweet milk:
the flocks give milk for the milking all the year round.
But while I roamed those countries gathering\nmuch substance, another man killed my brother —
by stealth, off guard, through\nthe treachery of his cursed wife.
So I take no joy in being lord of all this wealth.
You will have heard it from\nyour fathers, whoever they are:
I have suffered much, and I lost a house\nwell lived-in, full of many splendid things.
Would I lived here with a third part only of all this,\nand the men were alive who died in those years
in wide Troy, far from horse-grazing Argos!
And yet — though I mourn them all,\nand grieve, often, sitting here in our halls,
and one hour ease my heart with weeping, and the next\nleave off, for men are quickly sated of cold lament —
for all of them together I do not mourn so much,
grieved though I am, as for one man,\nwho makes sleep hateful to me,
and food, when I remember: for no Achaean labored as\nOdysseus labored and endured. And the end of it was
sorrow for him, and for me a grief never to be forgotten —\nthat he is gone so long, and we know nothing,
whether he lives or is dead. They must be mourning\nhim now, old Laertes, and steady-hearted Penelope,
and Telemachus, whom he left new-born in the house."
So he spoke, and stirred in the boy\nthe ache to weep for his father:
tears fell from his eyelids to\nthe ground at his father's name,
and he lifted the purple cloak before his eyes\nwith both hands. And Menelaus noticed him,
and pondered then in his mind and in his heart\nwhether to leave it to him to name his father,
or to question him first and test him point by point.
While he was turning this over\nin his mind and in his heart,
out of her fragrant high-roofed chamber came Helen,\nlooking like Artemis of the golden distaff;
and with her Adreste set out her well-made\nreclining chair, Alcippe brought a rug of soft wool,
and Phylo brought her silver basket, given her\nby Alcandre, wife of Polybus, who lived in Thebes
of Egypt, where the greatest wealth lies stored in houses:
he gave Menelaus two silver baths and a\npair of tripods and ten talents of gold;
and apart from these his wife gave\nHelen beautiful gifts of her own —
a golden distaff she gave, and a basket on wheels,\nsilver, its rims finished off in gold.
This the handmaid Phylo brought and set beside her,\nstuffed with fine-spun yarn, and across it
lay the distaff, wound with wool of violet darkness.
She sat down on the chair, with a footstool for her feet,
and at once began asking her husband about everything:
"Do we know yet, Menelaus, nurtured of Zeus, who these men
declare themselves to be, who have come to our house?
Shall I lie, or speak the truth? My heart bids me speak.
For never yet, I say, have I seen such a likeness,\nin man or woman — awe takes me, looking at him —
as this boy is like the son of great-hearted Odysseus:
Telemachus, whom that man left new-born in the house
when for my sake — bitch-faced that I was —\nyou Achaeans came up under Troy, with bold war in your hearts."
Then fair-haired Menelaus answered her:
"I too see it now, wife, just as you liken him:
those were the very feet of the man, the very hands,\nthe glance of his eyes, the head, the hair above.
And just now, remembering Odysseus,\nI was telling of all he labored and endured
for my sake — and the boy shed a\nbitter tear from under his brows,
holding the purple cloak up before his eyes."
Then Peisistratus, Nestor's son, answered him:
"Menelaus, son of Atreus, Zeus-nurtured, leader of\npeoples, this is indeed that man's son, as you say.
But he is modest, and his heart is shy of\nsplashing forth big words on a first arrival
in front of you, whose voice\ndelights us both like a god's.
Gerenian Nestor the horseman sent me out to\ncome with him as escort: he longed to see you,
in hope you might set some word or work before him.
For a son has many sorrows in the house when his\nfather is gone and no other helpers stand by him —
as now with Telemachus: the father gone,\nand no others in all the land to beat trouble away."
Then fair-haired Menelaus answered him:
"Well now! Truly the son of a beloved man is in my house,\na man who fought through many trials for my sake;
and I used to say that when he\ncame I would welcome him beyond all
the other Argives — if Olympian Zeus of the wide voice
gave the two of us a homecoming\nover the sea in our fast ships.
I would have settled him a city\nin Argos, and built him a house,
and brought him out of Ithaca with his goods and\nhis son and all his people — emptying out one town
of those that lie around and own me as their lord.
Being here, we would have mingled often; and nothing
would have parted us then,\nloving and delighting in each other,
until death's black cloud came folding round us.
But such things, I suppose,\nthe god himself must have grudged,
who made that unlucky man — him alone —\nthe man who never came home."
So he spoke, and stirred in them all the ache of lament.
Argive Helen wept, the daughter of Zeus,\nand Telemachus wept, and Menelaus, Atreus' son,
nor could the son of Nestor keep his eyes dry:
for his heart remembered blameless Antilochus,\nwhom the shining son of bright Dawn had killed.
Remembering him, he spoke winged words:
"Son of Atreus, old Nestor always said
you were clear-headed beyond other\nmortals, whenever we remembered you
in his halls, and questioned one another.
So now, if it may be, listen to me. I take no\npleasure in weeping after supper — and dawn
will come, early-born, soon enough. Not that I grudge\nlament for any mortal who dies and meets his doom:
this is the only honor left to miserable mortals,\nto cut a lock of hair and let a tear fall down the cheek.
For my brother died too — hardly the meanest of\nthe Argives. You would know him. I myself never
met him, never saw him. But beyond other men, they say,
Antilochus was surpassing swift of foot, and a fighter."
Then fair-haired Menelaus answered him:
"Dear friend — you have said all a clear-headed\nman could say or do, even a man older than you.
From such a father you come;\nhence your clear-headed speech.
Easily known is the seed of a\nman for whom the son of Cronos
spins out happiness at his marriage and his begetting —\nas now he has granted Nestor, through all his days,
to grow old sleek in his own halls,\nand his sons to be wise and the best of spearmen.
So we will let the weeping go, which came on us before,\nand think again of supper. Let them pour water
over our hands. And at dawn there will be tales again\nfor Telemachus and me to tell through to each other."
So he spoke, and Asphalion poured water over their\nhands, the busy henchman of glorious Menelaus,
and their hands went out to the\ngood things spread before them.
Then Helen, daughter of Zeus, thought of one thing more:
into the wine they were drinking\nshe straightway cast a drug
that undoes grief and anger and\nbrings forgetfulness of every evil.
Whoever swallowed it down, once mixed in the bowl,\nwould let no tear fall down his cheeks that day,
not though his mother and his father lay there dead,
not though before his face men put his brother or\nhis own son to the bronze, and his own eyes saw it.
Such were the subtle drugs the daughter of Zeus possessed,\ngood drugs, given her by Polydamna, wife of Thon,
the Egyptian — for there the grain-giving plowland bears
drugs in greatest plenty, many good in the mixing,\nmany baneful; and every man there is a healer beyond all
humankind: for they are of the race of Paeeon.
When she had cast it in, and bidden the wine be\npoured, she took up the talk again, and said:
"Menelaus, son of Atreus, nurtured of Zeus — and you,\nsons of good men. To this man and that Zeus gives
good and evil, now one, now another:\nfor he can do all things.
So now — feast where you sit in the halls
and take your pleasure in tales.\nAnd I will tell one that fits the hour.
All of it I could not tell, could not so much as number —\nall the trials of enduring-hearted Odysseus;
but here is one thing that mighty man did and dared
in the Trojans' country,\nwhere you Achaeans suffered your pains.
He beat his own body with disfiguring blows,\nthrew a foul rag over his shoulders, and like a house-slave
he slipped into the wide-wayed city of his enemies —\nhiding himself, in the likeness of another man,
a beggar: he who was nothing of\nthe kind by the Achaean ships.
In that shape he slipped into the\nTrojans' city, and all of them
were taken in. I alone knew him for what he was,
and questioned him; and he in\nhis cunning kept slipping away.
But when at last I was bathing\nhim and rubbing him with oil,
and had put clothes on him, and sworn a strong\noath not to reveal Odysseus to the Trojans
before he reached the fast ships and the huts,\nthen at last he told me all the Achaeans had in mind.
And he killed many Trojans with the long-edged bronze
on his way back to the Argives,\nand brought back a harvest of knowledge.
Then the other women of Troy wailed shrill. But my heart
rejoiced — for my heart had turned already toward going
home again, and I mourned too late the madness Aphrodite
gave me, when she led me there from my own dear country,
forsaking my child, my bridal chamber,\nand a husband lacking nothing, in mind or in beauty."
Then fair-haired Menelaus answered her:
"Yes, wife: all this you have\ntold rightly, in due measure.
By now I have learned the counsel and the mind of\nmany heroes, and traveled over much of the earth,
but never yet have my eyes looked on such a\none as the heart of enduring-hearted Odysseus.
Here is one more thing that mighty man did and dared\ninside the carved horse, where we sat, all the best
of the Argives, carrying death and doom to the Trojans.
Then you came there — some spirit must have moved you,\none that willed to hand glory to the Trojans —
and godlike Deiphobus came following after you.
Three times you circled the hollow ambush, stroking it,\nand you called by name the best of the Danaans,
making your voice the voice of each Argive's wife.
And I and the son of Tydeus and noble Odysseus,\nsitting in the middle of them, heard you calling;
and the two of us were wild to spring up\nand come out, or answer at once from within.
But Odysseus held us down,\nand checked us for all our longing.
Then all the other sons of the Achaeans kept silence;\nAnticlus alone was bent on giving you an answer —
but Odysseus clamped his great hands over his mouth
and held them there, unyielding,\nand saved all the Achaeans:
he held him so until Pallas Athena led you away."
Then clear-headed Telemachus answered him:
"Menelaus, son of Atreus,\nZeus-nurtured, leader of peoples —
the more grief: for none of this kept bitter death from him,\nnot though the heart inside him had been iron.
But come — send us to bed now, so that at last\nwe may lie down and take our joy of sweet sleep."
So he spoke; and Argive Helen ordered the slave-women
to set out bedsteads under the porch, and to lay on\nthem beautiful purple blankets, and spread rugs above,
and fleecy cloaks on top of all, for cover.
Out of the hall they went with torches in their hands\nand made the beds; and a herald led the guests out.
So they slept there in the forecourt of the house,\nthe hero Telemachus and Nestor's shining son;
but Atreus' son slept in the inner room of the high house,
and beside him lay long-robed Helen, shining among women.
When Dawn appeared, the early-born, with fingers of rose,
Menelaus of the great war-cry rose up from his bed,
put on his clothes, slung his\nsharp sword about his shoulder,
bound the beautiful sandals beneath his shining feet,\nand came out of his bedroom looking like a god.
He sat down beside Telemachus,\nand spoke a word, and named him:
"What need has brought you here, hero Telemachus,\nto shining Lacedaemon, over the broad back of the sea?
A public matter or private?\nTell me the plain truth of it."
Then clear-headed Telemachus answered him:
"Menelaus, son of Atreus,\nZeus-nurtured, leader of peoples,
I came in hope you might tell me some word of my father.
My house is being eaten; my rich fields are ruined;\nthe house is packed with enemies, who day upon day
slaughter my thronging flocks and\nmy shambling crook-horned cattle —
my mother's suitors, with their overweening insolence.
That is why I come now to your knees: in hope you will\nconsent to tell his bitter death — whether you saw it
with your own eyes, or heard the tale of him from another
wanderer. Beyond all men his mother bore him for sorrow.
Do not soften anything from courtesy or pity:
tell me fully whatever sight you came upon.
I beg you — if ever my father, good Odysseus,\npromised you word or work and made it good
in the Trojans' country,\nwhere you Achaeans suffered your pains,
remember it for me now: tell me the unerring truth."
Then fair-haired Menelaus, greatly stirred, replied:
"Shame on them! Truly in the bed of a strong-hearted man
they want to lie — the spineless creatures that they are!
As when a deer beds down her newborn suckling\nfawns in the thicket-lair of a mighty lion,
and goes questing the spurs and grassy hollows,\ngrazing — and then the lion comes back to his own bed
and lets an ugly doom loose on them both:
so Odysseus will let an ugly doom loose on those men.
If only — father Zeus, Athena, Apollo! —\nthe man he was long ago in strong-founded Lesbos,
when he rose on a challenge and wrestled Philomeleides\nand threw him hard, and all the Achaeans cheered:
such as he was then, let that\nOdysseus close with the suitors:
quick would their fates be then,\nand bitter their weddings.
As for what you ask of me and beg me: I will not talk\naround it, swerving aside, and I will not deceive you.
What the unerring Old Man of the Sea told me,\nnot one word of it will I hide or cover from you.
In Egypt the gods still held me, hungry as I was for home,
because I had not offered them their full hecatombs —
and the gods will always have\ntheir commandments remembered.
Now there is an island in the much-surging sea\noff the mouth of Egypt — Pharos, men call it,
as far out as a hollow ship runs in a whole\nday with a whistling wind astern of her —
and in it a harbor, good anchorage, from which men launch
their trim ships to sea, once they have drawn black water.
There the gods held me twenty days: never once\nthe sea-winds blowing fair, that speed ships
over the broad back of the sea.
And now all our stores would have\nbeen spent, and the men's strength,
had not one of the gods pitied me and saved me:
the daughter of mighty Proteus, the Old Man of the Sea —\nEidothea. For I stirred her heart beyond the rest
when she met me wandering alone,\napart from my companions —
for they were forever roving round the island,\nfishing with bent hooks, their bellies pinched with hunger.
She stood close by me and spoke, and said:
'Are you a fool, stranger — so slack, so loose of wit?
Or do you slacken by choice, and enjoy your suffering?
So long you are held on the island, and can find no\nending of it, while your companions' hearts grow small.'
So she spoke, and I answered her:
'I will say this straight,\nwhichever of the goddesses you are:
I am not held here by any will of mine. I must have\nsinned against the deathless ones who hold wide heaven.
But tell me — for the gods know all things — which of\nthe immortals shackles me here and has bound my road,
and my homecoming — how I shall\ngo over the fish-filled sea.'
So I spoke, and the shining goddess answered at once:
'Then I will tell you, stranger, and tell you truly.
There haunts this place an unerring Old Man of the Sea,\ndeathless Proteus of Egypt, who knows the depths
of every sea — Poseidon's under-servant.
He, they say, is my father, who begot me.
If you could somehow set an ambush and take hold of him,
he would tell you the road,\nand the measures of your journey,
and your homecoming — how you\nshall go over the fish-filled sea.
And he would tell you too, Zeus-nurtured, if you wish,\nwhatever evil and good have been done in your halls
while you have been gone on your long and grinding road.'
So she spoke, and I answered her:
'Devise the ambush yourself, for this old god —\nor he will see me first, or know beforehand, and escape me.
A god is hard for a mortal man to master.'
So I spoke, and the shining goddess answered at once:
'Then I will tell you, stranger, and tell you truly.
When the sun bestrides the middle of heaven,\nthen the unerring Old Man of the Sea comes out of the water
under the West Wind's breath,\nhidden in the dark shiver of the sea,
and coming out he beds down under the hollow caves;
and around him seals, the brood\nof the sea's lovely daughter,
sleep in a crowd, come up out of the gray salt water,\nbreathing out the sharp smell of the deep brine.
There I will bring you at the showing of dawn and bed\nyou down in the row. Choose well three companions,
the best you have by the well-benched ships.
And I will tell you all the old man's tricks.
First he will count his seals, and go over them;\nand when he has told them off by fives and seen them all,
he will lie down in their midst,\nlike a herdsman in his flocks.
The moment you see him settled down,\nthen let strength and force be all your thought:
hold him there for all his struggling,\nhowever he strains to escape.
He will make trial of everything, turning into all things
that creep upon the earth —\ninto water, into god-kindled fire;
but hold him unshakably, and press him the harder.
And when at last he questions you with words himself,\nin the same shape you saw him settle to sleep,
then leave off your force, hero: set the old man loose,\nand ask him which of the gods bears hard on you,
and your homecoming — how you\nshall go over the fish-filled sea.'
So speaking she plunged under the surging sea.
And I went to the ships where they stood in the sand,\nand my heart ran dark with many things as I went.
And when I had come down to the ship and the sea,\nwe made our supper, and ambrosial night came on,
and we lay down to sleep on the surf-line of the sea.
When Dawn appeared, the early-born, with fingers of rose,\nI set out along the shore of the wide-wayed sea,
praying hard to the gods; and I took three companions,\nthe three I trusted most for every venture.
She meanwhile had slipped under the wide gulf of the\nsea and brought up out of the deep four sealskins,
all fresh-flayed: she was plotting\nan ambush against her own father.
She had scooped out beds in the sea-sand and sat\nthere waiting. And we came up close beside her,
and she bedded us down in the row,\nand threw a skin over each.
There our ambush would have been most horrible: the deadly
stench of the salt-bred seals ground us down horribly —
who would lay himself down beside a beast of the sea? —
but she herself saved us; she devised a great relief:
she brought ambrosia and set it under each man's nose,
breathing sweetness,\nand it killed the stench of the beast.
All the morning we waited, with enduring hearts,\nand the seals came crowding up out of the sea, and then
lay down in rows along the surf-line of the sea;
and at midday the old man came\nout of the sea, and found his fat
seals, and went over them all, and counted the number —
and among the beasts he counted us the first,\nhis heart never guessing the trick. Then he too lay down.
Then we rushed him with a shout, and threw our arms
around him; and the old man did not forget his cunning art,\nbut first he turned to a great-bearded lion,
and then to a serpent, a leopard, a huge boar;\nhe turned to running water, to a tree in towering leaf;
and we held on unshakably, with enduring hearts.
But when at last the old man wearied, for all his tricks,\nthen he questioned me with words, and said:
'Which of the gods, son of Atreus, laid the plan with you
to take me by ambush against my will? What do you need?'
So he spoke, and I answered him:
'You know, old man — why ask me sideways? —\nhow long I am held on this island, and can find
no ending of it, and the heart inside me grows small.
But tell me — for the gods know all things — which of\nthe immortals shackles me here and has bound my road,
and my homecoming — how I shall\ngo over the fish-filled sea.'
So I spoke, and he answered me at once:
'But you should have offered fair victims to Zeus and\nthe other gods before embarking, to come most quickly
to your own country, sailing the wine-dark sea.
For it is not your portion to see your own people,\nto reach your well-built house and your own fatherland,
before you go back again to the waters of Egypt,\nthe river fallen from Zeus, and offer holy hecatombs
to the deathless gods who hold wide heaven.
Then the gods will give you the road you long for.'
So he spoke, and my heart broke within me,\nbecause he sent me back over the misted sea
to Egypt again — the long and grinding road.
Even so I answered him and said:
'All this I will do, old man, just as you command.
But come, tell me this, and tell it to me truly:
did all the Achaeans come home unharmed in their ships,
all whom Nestor and I left\nbehind when we sailed from Troy?
Or did any die a bitter death aboard his ship,
or in the arms of his friends,\nonce he had wound the war to its end?'
So I spoke, and he answered me at once:
'Son of Atreus, why ask me this? You have no need to know,\nno need to learn my mind. Not long, I tell you,
will you keep from tears,\nonce you have heard the whole of it.
Many of them were broken, and many were left;\nbut of the leaders of the bronze-shirted Achaeans, two
alone died on the homeward way —\nthe fighting you saw yourself —
and one, still living somewhere,\nis held back on the wide sea.
Ajax was broken among his long-oared ships.
Poseidon drove him first against the great rocks\nof Gyrae — and yet he saved him from the sea;
and he would have escaped his doom,\nthough Athena hated him,
had he not flung out an overweening\nword in his great blindness:
he said it was in the gods' despite he\nhad escaped the great gulf of the sea.
Poseidon heard his loud boasting,\nand straightway took his trident in his massive hands
and struck the rock of Gyrae, and split it apart:
one part held its place,\nbut the broken piece fell in the sea —
the piece where Ajax sat when\nthe great blindness took him —
and it carried him down into the boundless surging deep.
So he died there, when he had drunk the salt water.
But your brother somehow slipped the fates,\nescaped them in his hollow ships: the lady Hera saved him.
Yet when he was all but come to the steep height\nof Malea, then a storm-wind snatched him up
and carried him, groaning heavily, over the fish-filled\nsea to the border of the country where Thyestes once
had his house, and now Thyestes' son Aegisthus lived.
But when from there too a safe homecoming showed,\nand the gods turned the wind fair, and they reached home —
oh, rejoicing he set foot on his fathers' land,\nand touched his country and kissed it: the hot tears
streamed from him, so glad he was to see his land.
But from a lookout a watchman saw him — posted there
by Aegisthus of the crooked counsels, who had promised him
two talents of gold for wages: a full year he had watched,
so the king might not slip past unseen\nand remember his fighting strength.
The man went with his news to the house,\nto the shepherd of the people,
and at once Aegisthus laid his treacherous craft:
he picked the twenty best men in the land
and set an ambush, and across the\nhall he ordered a feast made ready;
and then he went to summon Agamemnon,\nshepherd of the people,
with horses and chariots —\nand unspeakable things in his mind.
He led him up unwitting of his death, and killed him\nat the dinner — as a man cuts down an ox at the manger.
Not one of the companions of Atreus'\nson was left, who followed him,
and not one of Aegisthus' men:\nthey were killed in the halls.'
So he spoke, and my heart broke within me,\nand I wept, sitting there in the sand; my heart
had no more will to live and see the light of the sun.
But when I had had my fill of weeping and writhing,\nthen the unerring Old Man of the Sea said to me:
'No more now, son of Atreus, this long unbending weeping:\nwe shall find no cure in it. Quick as you can,
try how you may come back to your own fatherland.
Either you will find him alive — or Orestes
has already killed him first,\nand you may come in time for the burying.'
So he spoke; and the heart and the proud spirit in\nmy breast, for all my grieving, were warmed again,
and lifting my voice I spoke winged words to him:
'These men I now know of. But name the third man:
the one still living, held back on the wide sea —\nor dead. Grieved as I am, I want to hear it.'
So I spoke, and he answered me at once:
'The son of Laertes, whose home is in Ithaca.
I saw him on an island, letting the big tears fall,\nin the halls of the nymph Calypso, who holds him there
by force; and he cannot come to his own fatherland,\nfor he has no ships at hand, no oars, no companions
to carry him over the broad back of the sea.
But for you, Zeus-nurtured Menelaus, it is not fated\nto die in horse-grazing Argos and meet your doom:
the deathless ones will carry you to the Elysian plain
and the ends of the earth — where fair-haired\nRhadamanthus is, where life is easiest of all for men:
no snow, no heavy winter, never rain, but always\nOcean sends up the breath of the singing West Wind
to bring men coolness — because Helen is\nyours, and you are son-in-law to Zeus.'
So speaking he plunged under the surging sea.
And I went to the ships with my godlike companions,\nand my heart ran dark with many things as I went.
We made our supper, and ambrosial night came on,
and we lay down to sleep on the surf-line of the sea.
When Dawn appeared, the early-born, with fingers of rose,
first of all we hauled our ships\ndown to the bright salt water
and set the masts and the sails in the trim ships,
and the men came aboard and took\ntheir places at the oarlocks,
and sitting in order they struck\nthe gray salt water with their oars.
Back to Egypt I brought the ships, to the river\nfallen from Zeus, and I offered the full hecatombs;
and when I had put to rest the\nanger of the gods who are forever,
I heaped a mound for Agamemnon,\nthat his fame might never be quenched.
That done, I sailed for home, and the immortals gave me
a wind, and brought me quickly to my own dear country.
But come now — stay on in my halls\nuntil the eleventh day, or the twelfth;
then I will send you off with honor,\nand give you shining gifts:
three horses and a polished chariot; and besides I\nwill give you a beautiful cup, so that you may pour
to the deathless gods and remember me all your days."
Then clear-headed Telemachus answered him:
"Son of Atreus, do not hold me here for long.
A year I could gladly sit here at your side\nand no ache for home or parents would take me:
such strange delight I have in hearing your tales\nand your words. But my companions chafe already
in holy Pylos, and you would hold me long here.
As for the gift you would give me —\nlet it be some treasure.
The horses I will not take to\nIthaca: I will leave them here
for you, for your own glory. For you are lord of a\nwide plain, where lotus grows in plenty, and galingale,
and wheat and spelt and broad white barley.
In Ithaca there are no wide courses, no meadowland at all:
goat-pasture — and lovelier to me than horse-pasture.
Not one of the islands that lean on\nthe sea is fit for driving horses,
or rich in meadows — and Ithaca beyond them all."
So he spoke; and Menelaus of the great war-cry smiled,
and stroked him with his hand,\nand spoke a word, and named him:
"You are of good blood, dear child — such things you say!
Then I will change the gifts for you; well I can.
Of all the treasures lying stored in my house I\nwill give you the most beautiful, the most honored:
I will give you a wrought mixing-bowl —\nall silver it is, and its rims are finished off in gold —
the work of Hephaestus. The hero Phaedimus gave it,\nking of the Sidonians, when his house sheltered me
on my way home there. This I would send with you."
So the two of them spoke such things to one another,\nwhile the feasters came up to the godlike king's house,
driving sheep before them,\ncarrying wine that puts heart in men,
and their fair-veiled wives sent bread along with them.
But the suitors, in front of Odysseus' hall,\nwere amusing themselves with discus and javelin throws
on the leveled ground, insolent as ever,\nwhere they always played.
There Antinous sat, and godlike Eurymachus,\nchiefs of the suitors, in prowess far the best of them all.
To them Noemon, Phronius' son,\ncame up and questioned Antinous, and said:
"Antinous, do we know at all — or not —\nwhen Telemachus comes back from sandy Pylos?
He went off with my ship, and now I need her
to cross to Elis of the wide\ndancing-grounds, where I keep twelve
brood mares, with hard-working mules at the teat,\nunbroken: I would drive one off and break him in."
So he spoke, and their hearts were\nastonished: they had never thought
he had gone to Neleian Pylos —\nsurely he was somewhere near,
out at the farms with the flocks, or with the swineherd.
Then Antinous, Eupeithes' son, answered him:
"Tell me the truth of it:\nwhen did he go, and what young men
went with him? Picked men of Ithaca — or his own\nhired hands and slaves? He could manage even that!
And tell me this too, honestly, so that I may know it:
did he take the black ship from\nyou by force, against your will,
or did you give it freely,\nbecause he begged you with fine words?"
Then Noemon, Phronius' son, answered him:
"I gave it freely, myself. What would any man do\nwhen such a man, with cares heavy on his heart,
asked? It would be hard to refuse the gift.
The young men who went with him are the best in the\nland after ourselves. And for their leader I marked
Mentor going aboard — or a god, the very image of him.
But here is what I wonder at: I saw noble Mentor
yesterday at dawn, right here —\nand he had boarded the ship for Pylos."
So he spoke, and went away to his father's house.
And the proud hearts of the two of them were stunned.
They sat the suitors down in a body and stopped their\ngames, and among them spoke Antinous, Eupeithes' son,
in anger: his black-brimming heart was hugely filled\nwith fury, and his eyes were like blazing fire:
"Damn it all — a great work insolently accomplished,
this voyage of Telemachus!\nAnd we said it would come to nothing.
In the teeth of all of us, a mere boy has simply gone:
hauled down a ship, and picked the best men in the land.
He will begin to be our ruin, and soon. May Zeus
destroy his strength before he\nreaches the measure of manhood!
But come, give me a fast ship and twenty companions,\nso I may watch for him and ambush him on his way home,
in the strait between Ithaca and rugged Samos —
so this sailing after his father\nmay cost him grim and dear."
So he spoke, and they all approved it and urged it on.
They rose at once and went into the house of Odysseus.
Nor was Penelope long in ignorance of the schemes\nthe suitors were brewing deep in their hearts:
for the herald Medon told her,\nwho had overheard their plans,
standing outside the court while\nthey wove their plot within.
He went through the house to bring the news to Penelope,
and as he crossed the threshold Penelope said to him:
"Herald, why have the lordly suitors sent you in?
To tell the slave-women of godlike Odysseus to\nleave their work and make the feast ready for them?
May they never woo again, never gather anywhere else —\nmay this be the last supper they ever eat here,
they who swarm in day after day and shear away the living,
the substance of clear-headed\nTelemachus! Did you never hear,
in years gone by, when you were\nchildren, from your fathers,
what kind of man Odysseus was\namong your parents' generation?
Never a deed out of measure, never an unjust word in\nall the land — though that is the way of godlike kings:
one mortal a king will hate, another he may love;\nbut that man never did outrage to a single soul.
No — your hearts are on show, and your ugly works:
there is no gratitude left,\nafterward, for good deeds done."
Then Medon answered her, a man of clear-headed sense:
"Would to god, my queen, that this were the worst of it.
A greater evil by far, and harder to bear,
the suitors are plotting now —\nmay the son of Cronos never accomplish it:
they are bent on cutting Telemachus\ndown with the sharp bronze
on his way home. He went for news of his father\nto holy Pylos and to shining Lacedaemon."
So he spoke, and there where she stood\nher knees went loose, and her heart;
for a long time speechlessness held her words; her eyes
filled up with tears; the flower of her voice was stopped.
At long last she found words to answer him:
"Herald, why is my child gone? There was no need to\nboard the fast-running ships, that are men's horses
of the salt water, and cross the great wet waste.
Is it so that not even his name should be left among men?"
Then Medon answered her, a man of clear-headed sense:
"I do not know whether some god stirred him,\nor whether his own heart drove him to go to Pylos, to learn
either his father's homecoming, or what doom he met."
So he spoke, and went away down\nthrough the house of Odysseus.
And heart-eating anguish poured\naround her; she could no longer
bear to sit on a chair, though the house was full of them,
but sank down on the threshold\nof her richly-worked chamber,
moaning pitiably; and around her whimpered the slave-women,\nall of them, young and old, that the house held.
And sobbing hard, Penelope said among them:
"Hear me, dear women. The Olympian has given me sorrows
beyond all the women who were bred and born beside me.
Long ago I lost my noble husband, the lion-hearted,\ngraced among the Danaans with every excellence,
that noble man, whose fame goes wide\nthrough Hellas and the heart of Argos.
And now again the storm-winds\nhave snatched my beloved son,
without glory, out of these halls,\nand I never heard him go.
Hard-hearted! Not even you — not one of you —\nthought to wake me from my bed, though your hearts knew well
the hour he went down to the black hollow ship.
If I had learned that he was pondering this journey,
then either he would have stayed,\nfor all his hunger for the road,
or he would have left me dead in these halls behind him.
But now let someone run and call old Dolius, my slave,\nwhom my father gave me when I first came here,
who keeps my orchard of many trees — so that quickly\nhe may go sit beside Laertes and tell him all of it.
Perhaps Laertes may weave some plan in his heart,\nand come out and weep before the people, who are bent
on destroying his line and the line of godlike Odysseus."
Then the dear nurse Eurycleia said to her:
"Dear bride — kill me with the pitiless bronze
or leave me in the house,\nbut I will not hide the story from you.
I knew all of it. I gave him what he ordered,\nbread and sweet wine. And he took a great oath from me
not to tell you before the twelfth day came,\nor you missed him yourself and heard that he was gone —
so you would not mar your lovely skin with weeping.
Now bathe, and take clean clothing for your body,\nand go up to your upper room with your attendant women,
and pray to Athena, daughter of aegis-bearing Zeus:
she may yet save him, even out of death itself.
And do not grieve a grieving old man more.\nI cannot think the blessed gods have wholly hated the line
of Arceisius' son: someone will yet be left to hold\nthe high-roofed house and the fat fields far around."
So she spoke, and lulled her lament,\nand stayed her eyes from weeping.
And she bathed, and took clean clothing for her body,
and went up to her upper room with her attendant women,
and set the barley-grains in a\nbasket, and prayed to Athena:
"Hear me, child of aegis-bearing Zeus, Unwearied One.
If ever Odysseus of the many designs, in these halls,\nburned fat thigh-cuts of ox or sheep for you,
remember them for me now: save my dear son,\nand beat away the suitors in their evil overbearing pride."
So she cried the ritual cry;\nand the goddess heard her prayer.
But the suitors broke into\nuproar through the shadowy halls,
and thus would one of the arrogant young men say:
"So the much-courted queen is making ready a marriage
for one of us — and knows nothing\nof the death prepared for her son."
So they would say — knowing nothing of what was prepared.
And Antinous addressed them all, and said:
"Fools! Keep clear of overweening talk of any\nkind — or someone may carry the word inside.
Up now, in silence, and let us accomplish\nthe plan that pleased us all in our hearts."
So he spoke, and picked the twenty best men,
and they went down to the fast\nship and the sand-beach of the sea.
First of all they hauled the ship down to deep water,\nand set the mast and the sails in the black ship,
and fitted the oars into their leather slings,\nall in due order, and spread the white sails open;
and high-spirited henchmen carried down their arms.
They moored her well out in the water, and came ashore,
and there they took their supper,\nand waited for evening to come.
But she in her upper room, watchful-minded Penelope,\nlay fasting, tasting neither food nor drink,
turning it over: whether her blameless son would escape\ndeath, or be broken under the overweening suitors.
As a lion turns and turns amid a crowd of men,\nin dread, as they draw the treacherous circle round him,
so she was turning when the deep sleep came upon her;
and she sank back and slept,\nand all her joints went loose.
Then the goddess thought of one\nthing more, gray-eyed Athena.
She made a phantom, fashioned in the likeness of a woman —\nIphthime, daughter of great-hearted Icarius,
wed to Eumelus, whose home was in Pherae —\nand sent it to the house of godlike Odysseus,
so that it might bring Penelope, weeping and mourning,\nsome pause from lamentation and tear-filled grief.
Into the chamber it came, past the strap of the bolt,\nand stood above her head, and said to her:
"Do you sleep, Penelope, your heart worn with grief?
No — the gods who live at ease will not have you weep\nand be anguished: for your son has his homecoming
still; he is no sinner in the sight of the gods."
Then watchful-minded Penelope answered her —\nslumbering very sweetly at the gates of dream:
"Why have you come here, sister? You have not\nbeen used to come before: your home is far away.
And you bid me leave off my misery and all\nthe pains that crowd my mind and heart.
Long ago I lost my noble husband, the lion-hearted,\ngraced among the Danaans with every excellence,
that noble man, whose fame goes wide\nthrough Hellas and the heart of Argos.
And now again my beloved son has gone in a hollow ship,
a mere boy, unpracticed in\nhardships and the meetings of men.
It is for him I mourn even more than for that other;
for him I tremble, for him I fear,\nthat something may strike him,
whether among the men of the land\nhe has gone to, or on the sea.
For many enemies are scheming against him, hungry to\nkill him before he comes back to his own country."
And the dim phantom answered her:
"Take heart. Do not fear too greatly in your mind.
Such an escort goes with him as other men have prayed\nto have stand beside them — for she has power —
Pallas Athena. And she pities you your grieving:
it is she who sent me now to tell you this."
Then watchful-minded Penelope said to her:
"If you are truly a god,\nand have heard the voice of a god,
then come — tell me also of\nthat other, that man of sorrow:
does he live still somewhere,\nand see the light of the sun,
or is he dead already, down in the house of Hades?"
And the dim phantom answered her:
"Of him I will not tell the story through —
whether he lives or is dead.\nIt is evil to speak words empty as wind."
So speaking it slipped away by the doorpost bolt into\nthe breath of the winds. And the daughter of Icarius
started up out of sleep, and her heart was warmed:
so vivid a dream had rushed upon\nher in the dark hour of the night.
But the suitors had embarked,\nand were sailing the watery ways,
turning over in their hearts sheer murder for Telemachus.
There is a rocky island in the middle of the sea,\nmidway between Ithaca and rugged Samos —
Asteris, no great place; but there are harbors in it
fit for ships to lurk in, open at either end.\nThere the Achaeans waited in ambush.
